question: What happened to the people who carry words between languages when machines were expected to replace them, and which part of the work stays with people, and for how long?

issues.note: Hard cut from the desk monitor to the library street while the opening question is still on screen. The subtitle lingers across the cut, so the shift to the lamplighter frame reads as abrupt.

The narration jumps from the video-call office back to 1954 with a 'courtroom booth to video call' line, and the picture goes to a dusk street. The 1954 callback is not shown (no computer or lab image), so it is confusing.

'One difference: in 1966, not good enough' is shown over the 1966 office with the translator's desk, which does not illustrate the point. The same office is then reused for the next two beats, so the picture does not support the narration.
'One machine: a database of sentences already translated' is shown over a generic office with a plant. Nothing on screen shows a database, so the narration and picture do not match.

'Where people used Google Translate more…' and the '≈28,000' card are shown over the same office, then cut to a stat card and a cross-dissolve that mixes the card with the office. The statistic's link to the narration is not clear and the dissolve is muddy.
The video-call interpreter shot holds across R15.6 to R16.3 (about 12 s) with only small changes (stat cards over the same frame). The picture stays nearly static.
From R17.6 to R18.7 the film sits on near-identical dusk street views (about 30 s) with only slight camera drift. This is a long hold on the closing image with little new to look at.
The monitor shot with 'a moment later, another language' repeats the same desk frame for about 12 s (R10.1 to R10.5). It is the same picture as R09.7 and R12.1.
